newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium wants Tractebel, Electrabel merger.
newsitem.headline: Belgium wants Tractebel, Electrabel merger.

text.p: The Belgian government is pushing for a merger of utility group Tractebel with its unit Electrabel in an operation which would be the largest in Brussels bourse history.
It could also lead to major changes in Belgium's business world.

A spokeswoman for Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said on Wednesday he had proposed the merger in talks with Etienne Davignon, head of Tractebel parent company Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB), and Gerald Mestrallet, head of SGB's French parent Compagnie de Suez.
She said SGB and Suez had no objection to such a merger.

"The government considers that in the long run a merger between Tractebel and Electrabel is the best way to safeguard Tractebel's autonomy and Belgian interests, notably in energy policy and employment," Dehaene said in a letter to Davignon.

A Tractebel-Electrabel merger would create a giant utility group whose 630 billion franc ($17.7 billion) stock market capitalisation would represent about one seventh of total Belgian market capitalisation.
The government's unusual request for a merger is its latest move in a series of measures aimed at boosting Tractebel's autonomy from its French shareholders.

The planned merger of Suez with French utility group Lyonnaise des Eaux has given rise to worries here that the new French utilities giant would suffocate Tractebel's international ambitions and become too dominant in Electrabel, which has a virtual monopoly on electricity production in Belgium.

At the instigation of the government, Tractebel will change its articles of incorporation on June 20 to transform the company into a so-called autonomous company, with more independence from its shareholders.

A merger with Electrabel would further dilute SGB's stake in Tractebel to about 25 percent. It now stands at 65 percent, but will fall to just over 50 percent when Tractebel's planned merger with its Powerfin unit is finalised in October.
SGB said it also wanted to keep the majority in a merged Tractebel-Electrabel.
"(SGB) wants to hold the majority in any possible new entity," an SGB spokesman told Reuters.

Some analysts expect that a Tractebel-Electrabel merger will be just a precursor to a merger of the new unit with SGB itself, in a move that would mimic the Suez-Lyonnaise operation and which would transform the entire Belgian financial market.

"This could be a forerunner for an operation like the Suez- Lyonnaise merger, whereby SGB merges with Tractebel-Electrabel in a daughter-eats-mother operation," said Stephane Van Nimmen, an analyst with brokerage Mignon, Hanart Declerck.

SGB is Belgium's largest and oldest holding company. Besides Tractebel, it controls Generale Bank and Fortis AG, the country's biggest bank and biggest insurance company, along with assets in the steel, chemical and non-ferrous metals sector.
A shake-up of SGB would be the equivalent of an earthquake on the Brussels bourse.
Before merging Suez with Lyonnaise, Mestrallet -- who is a former chief executive of SGB -- sold off most of Suez's assets.
Since announcing the Suez-Lyonnaise operation, Mestrallet has indicated that all SGB's assets, with the exception of Tractebel, could be sold.
SGB confirmed that it had no principal objection against a Tractebel-Electrabel merger.
"We are not against a merger between Tractebel and Electrabel, provided this is beneficial for both companies and all its shareholders," an SGB spokesman told Reuters.
He added that SGB would be willing to be diluted to less than 50 percent in the new unit as long as it remains the leading shareholder.
Tractebel shares ended 0.32 percent lower at 15,525 francs on a firmer Brussels bourse. Electrabel closed 0.64 percent lower at 7,790 francs.
